WIN — Customer was worried and uncertain about thermostat issue. You set clear boundaries immediately: 'I'm not gonna do any work without your approval' and 'goal is deliver five-star experience.' That calm, transparent expectation-setting reassured them right at the start. Trust foundation built early.

FIX — After explaining over-current issue and imminent compressor failure risk, should ask: 'The system shows it could fail anytime — would you like to get ahead of this with a replacement plan, or deal with it when it fails?' (Transcript cuts off; may have done this.)

WIN — When customer shared his wife passed in April, you paused with respect ('excuse me') instead of pushing through. That human moment shown at vulnerable time builds trust when the customer needs work done. Small gesture, big impact on rapport for major purchase decision.

FIX — Customer scoped work narrowly (insulation repair for home inspection) to close sale. Didn't explore: 'While we're up there, should we check the rest of the system? Addresses buyer concerns.' Missed full-system value opportunity at a transaction moment.

FIX — Move from diagnosis to decision faster—customer has high urgency (medical condition + failing system) but call ended before you explicitly asked which option they'd prefer or proposed scheduling the Comfort Advisor.

FIX — When the customer asked 'You'll be able to fix it?', you clarified what was available but didn't reconnect to their pain (AC down all day, inconvenience) with a choice question — move from 'depends on what you want' to 'here's what I'd do: Option 1 is the capacitor today for quick relief, Option 2 is a full upgrade for peace of mind — which matters more to you?' That question closes the visit.

WIN — Ben showed the soapy refrigerant and explained "This soap is going into your compressor...it's gonna burn up the whole entire system," proving the threat was real and unavoidable, which created the urgency that got them to schedule the sales consultation tomorrow.
FIX — When the customer said they'd been overcharged before, Robert missed reconnecting: asking 'What made that feel excessive?' would have rebuilt trust before presenting this $1,400 estimate.

WIN — Francisco reframed the replacement cost as monthly payments ($150–250) instead of a lump sum, moving the customer from cost-hesitant to genuinely interested in the replacement option and securing the estimate visit.

FIX — When customers said they'd run the compressor until it fails, Ben didn't reconnect to the emotional trigger. He should have asked: 'I know you mentioned a baby coming—how would you feel being without AC mid-summer if the compressor quits and we're waiting on a replacement unit?' This might have moved them from 'wait and see' to at least scheduling an install quote.
FIX — Need to present options and get approval to move forward; ensure customer understands next steps.
WIN — Presented options and secured approval; moving forward with solution.
WIN — Presented options and secured approval; moving forward with solution.

WIN— Masterclass in consultative selling under complex circumstances. You navigated the tenant/homeowner responsibility issue by first educating, then building trust, then guiding the decision. The key: when Nazareth hesitated on cost, you didn't push—you explained value instead. He felt heard, not sold. That's how consultative selling closes deals.

FIX — Present options before the report. Customer was engaged and concerns (about pricing) were real. Say upfront: 'I'm seeing two paths—replacement or having our Comfort Advisor scope all options. Which makes sense?' Commit to next step in the moment.

FIX — When the customer asked "You'll be able to fix it" you deflected by explaining what parts were needed to order, rather than asking a clarifying question to understand their real concern—cost, timeline, or long-term reliability. Ask "Are you most concerned about getting it running today, or do you want a permanent fix?" to reconnect and move toward a decision.

WIN — When the customer said "That's too much money" about the $8,500 repair, you didn't just accept it and move on—you reframed the entire value conversation. You explained why Sierra charges what it does: permits pulled by the city, proper electrical and gas work, warranty transfer to new owners. Then you asked the deciding question: "Is this a house you guys plan on keeping?" When they said they're selling very soon, you pivoted smoothly to replacement options with payment plans instead of fighting for a repair that wouldn't make sense for their timeline. That strategic listening and flexibility turned a potential walk-away into a scheduled specialist visit and genuine customer interest in exploring solutions.
WIN — Presented options and secured approval; moving forward with solution.

FIX — After finding rusted coils, damaged blower motor, and low refrigerant levels, didn't reconnect findings to urgency or frame clear options. Should have asked: 'Your system can fail anytime in summer heat — do you want to repair today or plan for replacement?'

WIN — Francisco diagnosed dead capacitor, loose fan motor bearings, and cautious compressor, then educated the customer on why builder-grade systems only last 8–12 years before "big stuff" fails; instead of just listing repairs, he explained the lifecycle so the customer could choose repair, wait, or replace with confidence.

WIN — Customer objected on price by comparing cheaper online units. Instead of defending cost, you reframed value: 'That's without refrigerant, installation, permits. We pull permits so the city inspects us. Your insurance covers it because we did it right.' Customer agreed to specialist estimate visit.

WIN — Diagnosed the exact problem with precise measurements (dead capacitor, 45.5 rated vs 12 on one side, 0 on other), then connected it to the bigger picture: 'Your system is builder-grade, so after 8-12 years you expect multiple failures.' This turned diagnosis into confidence in your solution.

WIN — Maintained professional, systematic approach throughout diagnostic. This consistency builds customer confidence. Continue that professional standard through options and close phases for best outcomes.
FIX — Ask clarifying questions early to fully understand the issue before proposing solutions.
FIX — Ask clarifying questions early to fully understand the issue before proposing solutions.

WIN — Francisco educated his way into urgency. He explained that R22 refrigerant laws changed in 2025, so the mismatched system (2017 indoor, 2022 outdoor) can't just be patched—it needs replacement. Then he immediately scheduled the install team for the same day or next day, turning a 'maybe I'll think about it' into a locked-in appointment. Customer moved from confused to committed.

WIN — Ben set crystal-clear expectations upfront: "I just need a quick tour, do a thorough evaluation, write the full report, show you pictures and videos, won't do any work without your approval, and this is all for a five-star experience." When the motor start device diagnosis came back, customers approved immediately because they trusted the process.
WIN — Rep converts lead-time uncertainty into trust by honest communication ('I don't want to promise next week then you wait three months'), making transparency a service value.

WIN— Strong FSG framework execution. You successfully navigated the complex customer concern (temperature variability affecting baby comfort) by asking clarifying questions, presenting actionable options, and building trust through patient explanation. Customers flip when they feel genuinely heard—not dismissed as trivial. Your deliver phase energy (5-star request) positioned Sierra as the expert to call back.

WIN— Masterclass in consultative selling. You turned a 127-minute deep-dive into qualified lead currency by educating the customer on thermal expansion and system design issues. Customers flip when they understand WHY problems matter, not just what problems exist. This builds trust for future callbacks.

FIX — Ben diagnosed the risk brilliantly (compressor noise, low refrigerant, R22 obsolete, leak risk) and presented two paths (proactive vs. reactive). But when the customer said 'I'll run it until it fails,' Ben didn't loop back to the emotional concern about the baby. A simple reconnect like 'Okay, so you're saying run until it breaks—and if that happens mid-summer with your newborn, we'd install a full system replacement. Want to get the install team to quote that now so you know the cost?' would have at least flipped this to an estimate.

FIX— Before presenting findings, set clear expectations: 'I'll evaluate both systems, then walk you through 2-3 options so you can choose what fits your budget.' This reduces cost anxiety and speeds the close.

FIX— Strong diagnostic and option presentation are undercut by incomplete close. When customers ask about warranty implications, immediately move to decision: 'Here's what I recommend: Given the system age, replacing the compressor with our warranty protection makes sense. I can schedule installation for tomorrow at 10 AM—does that work?' Lock in the commitment.

WIN — Francisco didn't let research stall the momentum. When the customer wanted to check with their warranty company first, instead of saying 'call us back,' Francisco immediately said 'let me schedule your appointment with the install team so you're locked in.' He converted a 'let me think about it' moment into a committed next step, turning a diagnostic call into an active lead.

FIX— Excellent discovery work was undermined by missing the close. After thorough assessment, create decision options: 'Option A is a high-efficiency upgrade with better modulation. Option B is a maintenance plan for your current system. Which direction appeals to you?' Then ask for commitment.

FIX — When the customer asked 'can you fix it?', ask a clarifying question about priorities (budget vs. reliability, immediate vs. long-term) instead of only listing constraints — that's the moment to move toward scheduling the return visit.

FIX — When the customer mentioned the previous technician overcharging him, that was an objection you needed to address with empathy and a reconnecting question: 'What's reasonable for you to get this reliable again?' That's how you move from evaluation to closing a decision.

FIX — Diagnosed three major issues (dead capacitor, failing fan motor, questionable compressor) but didn't frame them as clear decision pathways. Should have said: 'Option A: quick fix for capacitor alone; Option B: both items for reliability; Option C: replacement for long-term peace of mind.'
FIX — When they said they'd wait til end of summer because of cost, you didn't ask: 'If we lock in $170/month now, would that move your timeline sooner?' That's your reconnect to the real objection.

FIX — When the customer said 'I'm gonna hold off,' you explained why other estimates would be the same instead of asking 'What's your biggest concern—the price, the timeline, or something else?' That empathetic check-in question might have revealed whether financing, a sooner appointment, or clarifying the warranty would have changed their mind.

WIN — When the customer's cost objection could have shut the door ("You expecting me to shield $10,000?"), you opened it back up by offering phased options: "there's options, there's not it doesn't have to be $10,000, there's options that you can do" — turning resistance into the entry point for the estimate visit and repair TGL.
